howTo.title: How it works
howTo.subtitle: From zero to a production adapter, in six steps
howTo.s1Body: GIGO transforms your data with the AI engine of your choice (OpenAI or Anthropic), using YOUR API key: you keep full control over usage and billing. The key is encrypted and never shown in clear text again.
howTo.s1LinkSuffix: and paste the key of the provider you want to use.
howTo.s2Body: One adapter = one output format. You configure no rules: just paste an example of the JSON your destination tool expects.
howTo.s2Body2: Another option: paste the target API's documentation in the “From Docs (AI)” tab and the format is inferred automatically. Then pick the AI engine and give it a name.
howTo.s3Body: On the adapter page, paste “dirty” data into the playground and run it: you see the transformed output, latency, token usage and the model used. Iterate on your format example until the result is exactly right.
howTo.s4Body: Each adapter exposes a unique webhook URL: configure it in the source tool (form, e-commerce, CRM…) or call it directly. The X-Webhook-Secret header protects the endpoint, and each adapter has its own per-minute rate limit.
howTo.s4Email: You can also send or forward an email to the adapter's dedicated address (shown on its page): the email body and its JSON/CSV attachments go through the same pipeline.
howTo.s5Body: Configure the destination URL and its authentication (Bearer, API key, Basic, credentials are AES-256-GCM encrypted): every transformed payload is delivered automatically. Without a destination, the webhook response carries the result.
howTo.s6Body: The activity log traces every transformation: input, output, duration, tokens, errors. Filter, inspect the details, and replay a failed transformation in one click after fixing, without asking the source to resend.
howTo.tip1: Use realistic values in your format example: they teach the AI the expected types (“4990” → number, “jean@example.com” → email).
howTo.tip2: Always enable the webhook secret before exposing a URL to the internet, it's generated in one click on the adapter page.
howTo.tip3: Unsure about a mapping? The playground is frustration-free: test your edge cases there before wiring the real source.

learnings.title: Learnings
learnings.help: The adapter learns from its runs: validated fixes become reference examples, detected mistakes become constraints, injected into future transformations.
learnings.empty: Nothing learned yet. Replay a fixed failure, or promote a successful log to an example from the activity log : the adapter will remember.

hero.title: Your data arrives messy.
hero.sub: GIGO is a universal adapter. It takes data exactly as the source sends it, works out what it contains, and rewrites it into the precise structure your tool expects.
hero.note: Your model keys stay yours, encrypted at rest and never shared.

notes.n1a: Reference cleaned up, spacing and casing normalised
notes.n1b: Local date format converted to ISO 8601
notes.n1c: Displayed amount converted to integer cents
notes.n2a: Priority inferred from the tone of the message
notes.n2b: Order reference pulled out of free text
notes.n2c: Phone number normalised to international format
notes.n3b: Units stripped, values converted to numbers
notes.n3c: Timestamp rebuilt with its time zone

problem.title: The API is not the hard part, the format is
problem.body: Every source speaks its own dialect: local date formats, amounts written as text, inconsistent casing, nested fields, stray keys. Every destination demands another one. Seven sources and five destinations means thirty five integrations to write, test and maintain.
problem.bodyTwo: One adapter in the middle brings that down to twelve connections. That is the only job GIGO has, and it does it without you writing a single transformation rule.

how.title: Four steps, no rules to write
how.s1Body: Webhook, forwarded email or direct paste: data comes in through whichever channel suits you.
how.s2Body: The model reads the raw payload and works out what it holds, with no hand written mapping.
how.s3Body: Output is constrained by your target schema. The model cannot invent a field.
how.s4Body: The result is sent to your destination, with logs, replay and statistics.
how.inputsLabel: Three ways to send data in

guarantees.title: An integration tool, not an AI demo
guarantees.c1Body: The target schema is imposed on the model. When in doubt the call fails loudly instead of returning something wrong.
guarantees.c2Body: Every run is traced: input, output, latency, cost. A failed run replays in one click.
guarantees.c3Body: You connect your own OpenAI or Anthropic key. It is encrypted at rest and never leaves your account.
guarantees.c4Body: Destinations checked against SSRF attacks, per user data isolation, 110 automated tests.

learning.title: The adapter learns from its own runs
learning.body: A validated transformation becomes a reference example. A detected mistake becomes a constraint. Both go back into the prompt of later runs: the adapter gets sharper the more it works, without anyone rewriting a rule.
learning.bodyTwo: That is the difference between a tool that repeats the same mistake every week and a tool that fixes it once.
learning.exampleNote: Successful replay of a transformation that had failed
learning.pitfallBody: Never output these keys, they are not in the target schema: internal_notes, raw_payload.
learning.pitfallNote: Captured after an output that left the schema
learning.f1Body: Two triggers: a transformation that used to fail and now passes becomes an example, a key invented by the model becomes a constraint.
learning.f2Body: Five examples and eight constraints per adapter at most, and the three newest examples plus five newest constraints go into the prompt. Memory never inflates your cost.
learning.f3Body: Every learning can be disabled or deleted, a successful log is promoted to an example in one click, and the playground replays the same payload with and without, to compare.
learning.f4Body: Changing the target schema disables examples that went stale, and learned data is fenced off from the rest of the prompt so it cannot give the model instructions.

openSource.title: The code is readable, the deployment is yours
openSource.body: GIGO is published under the MIT licence. Audit it, host it yourself with Docker, adapt it to your needs. No lock in, no captive data.

final.title: Try it with your own data
final.body: Paste a properly messy payload, describe the structure you expect, watch what comes out.

declaration.title: You do not describe the rule, you show the result
declaration.body: Nobody writes a mapping. You paste an example of what you want out, GIGO derives the target schema from it, and that schema becomes the constraint the model has to satisfy on every run.
declaration.note: The schema stays editable by hand at any time.
